title: What are the requirements for effective partitioning — align with query access patterns + use low-cardinality columns — and what goes wrong with high-cardinality partition columns (millions of tiny directories, metadata bloat, small-file problem, driver OOM)?
shortTitle: Requirements for effective partitioning and the high-cardinality pitfall

s1_definition.profdef: Effective write-time partitioning requires two things: the partition column must match how queries actually filter the data (align with access patterns), and it must be low cardinality so each partition directory holds a meaningful amount of data. Choosing a high-cardinality column such as account id or timestamp creates an enormous number of directories, each holding almost nothing, which produces metadata bloat in the catalog and file system, the small-file problem that cripples read performance, and can make the driver run out of memory while listing or planning over millions of directories.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, partitioning is like deciding how to label filing drawers. Labelling by branch — a handful of values — gives a few full, useful drawers that auditors actually ask for. But labelling by individual account number gives you millions of drawers each holding one slip, so the records room is overwhelmed with empty folders, the index of drawers becomes a book nobody can carry, and the clerk collapses trying to even list them all. Good labels are few and match the questions people ask.
s1_definition.oneliner: Partition by low-cardinality columns you actually filter on; partitioning on a high-cardinality column explodes into millions of tiny directories and crashes planning.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Effective write-time partitioning requires two things: the partition column must match how queries actually filter the data (align with access patterns), and it must be low cardinality so each partition directory holds a meaningful amount of data. Choosing a high-cardinality column such as account id or timestamp creates an enormous number of directories, each holding almost nothing, which produces metadata bloat in the catalog and file system, the small-file problem that cripples read performance, and can make the driver run out of memory while listing or planning over millions of directories.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, partitioning is like deciding how to label filing drawers. Labelling by branch — a handful of values — gives a few full, useful drawers that auditors actually ask for. But labelling by individual account number gives you millions of drawers each holding one slip, so the records room is overwhelmed with empty folders, the index of drawers becomes a book nobody can carry, and the clerk collapses trying to even list them all. Good labels are few and match the questions people ask.

**One line to remember:** Partition by low-cardinality columns you actually filter on; partitioning on a high-cardinality column explodes into millions of tiny directories and crashes planning.

sections.s2_technical:
The first requirement is alignment with access patterns. Partitioning only helps when queries filter on the partition column, because that is what enables partition pruning. If you partition by branch but every query filters by date, the partitioning does nothing for pruning and you have paid the organizational cost for no benefit. So you choose the partition column by studying how the data is queried, and you put the most frequently filtered column first in a multi-column partition.

The second requirement is low cardinality. Cardinality is the number of distinct values. A good partition column has few distinct values relative to the data size, so each directory ends up with a healthy amount of data — ideally at least a few hundred megabytes, the size that columnar formats like Parquet read efficiently. Branch, country, region, product type, and date at the day or month grain are typical good choices.

When you partition on a high-cardinality column, several things break at once. First, directory explosion: partitioning by account id with ten million accounts creates ten million directories. Second, the small-file problem: each directory holds a tiny sliver of data, so you write millions of tiny files, and tiny files defeat columnar read efficiency and overwhelm object stores and HDFS, which charge a fixed cost per file. Third, metadata bloat: the metastore or file listing must track millions of partitions, which slows every query's planning phase. Fourth, driver out-of-memory: Spark lists and holds partition metadata on the driver, and millions of partitions can exhaust the driver heap during planning, failing the job before any real work starts.

A senior-level nuance is the fix. For high-cardinality keys you do not partition; you bucket, which uses a fixed number of files via hashing and gives join and aggregation benefits without directory explosion. You can also partition on a low-cardinality derived column — for example, partition by month instead of exact timestamp, or by a hash bucket of the account id — so you keep pruning benefits with a controlled directory count. The general guideline many teams use is to keep the number of partitions in the thousands at most, not millions, and to ensure each partition holds roughly 128 megabytes to 1 gigabyte.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A junior engineer at the National Bank of India partitions the transactions table by account id to "make lookups fast." The bank has ten million accounts, so the write creates ten million directories each holding a few rows. The next day's job fails on the driver with an out-of-memory error while listing partitions, and reads are painfully slow because of millions of tiny files. This is exactly the high-cardinality pitfall.

Problem 2 — The fix is to partition by a low-cardinality column aligned with queries. Most reports filter by branch and month, both low cardinality, so partitioning by branch and month gives a few thousand healthy directories and enables pruning. For account-level lookups, bucketing by account id is used instead.

The demo computes, for several candidate partition columns, the number of directories, the average bytes per directory, and whether the layout is healthy or dangerous, logging a recommendation and flagging the driver-OOM risk for high-cardinality choices.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/spark-partition-design-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.PartitionDesignDemo

# In a real Spark job:
#   # GOOD: low cardinality, aligned with queries
#   txns.write.partitionBy("branch", "txnMonth").parquet("s3://bank/txns")
#   # BAD: high cardinality → millions of dirs, driver OOM
#   # txns.write.partitionBy("accountId").parquet(...)   # DON'T
#   # For account lookups use bucketing instead:
#   txns.write.bucketBy(256, "accountId").saveAsTable("txns_bucketed")
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 2 TB transactions dataset and five candidate partition columns with different cardinalities and query alignment.

Step 1: The evaluator checks account id, which has ten million distinct values. That far exceeds the safe partition ceiling, so it flags DANGER — directory explosion, tiny files, and driver out-of-memory risk.

Step 2: It checks the transaction timestamp, which has even higher cardinality, and flags the same danger — this is the worst possible choice.

Step 3: It checks branch, which has 500 distinct values. Dividing 2 TB by 500 gives about 4 GB per directory, well above the 128 MB floor, and branch is queried often, so it returns GOOD.

Step 4: It checks transaction month, 36 distinct values, giving large healthy directories and aligned with queries, so it returns GOOD.

Step 5: It checks customer name, which is high cardinality and not filtered by queries, so it returns AVOID because partitioning would give no pruning benefit anyway.

Step 6: The demo logs each verdict at the appropriate level and recommends partitioning by branch and month while bucketing by account id for lookups.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:28:05 [SEVERE] DANGER: 'accountId' has 10000000 distinct values → directory explosion, tiny files, DRIVER OOM risk
2026-10-30 04:28:05 [SEVERE] DANGER: 'txnTimestamp' has 86400000 distinct values → directory explosion, tiny files, DRIVER OOM risk
2026-10-30 04:28:05 [INFO] GOOD: 'branch' — 500 dirs, ~4096 MB each, aligned with queries
2026-10-30 04:28:05 [INFO] GOOD: 'txnMonth' — 36 dirs, ~56888 MB each, aligned with queries
2026-10-30 04:28:05 [WARNING] AVOID: 'customerName' is not filtered by queries — partitioning gives no pruning
2026-10-30 04:28:05 [INFO] Recommendation: partitionBy("branch", "txnMonth"); bucket by accountId for lookups.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Effective partitioning rests on two requirements. First, the partition column must align with how queries actually filter the data, because partitioning only pays off through pruning, and pruning only happens when queries filter on the partition column. If I partition by branch but everyone queries by date, I have paid the cost and gained nothing. Second, the column must be low cardinality so each directory holds a healthy amount of data — ideally a few hundred megabytes up to a gigabyte, which is the range columnar formats read efficiently. Branch, region, product type, and date at a month grain are typical good choices.

The failure mode is partitioning on a high-cardinality column like account id or exact timestamp. Several problems hit at once. You get directory explosion, because ten million accounts means ten million directories. You get the small-file problem, because each directory holds almost nothing, and tiny files defeat columnar reads and overwhelm the object store with fixed per-file costs. You get metadata bloat, because the catalog and file listing must track millions of partitions, slowing every query's planning. And worst of all you can get a driver out-of-memory failure, because Spark holds partition metadata on the driver and millions of partitions exhaust its heap during planning, so the job dies before doing any real work.

I saw exactly this at the National Bank of India when someone partitioned the transactions table by account id and the next day's job died on the driver with an out-of-memory error. We fixed it by partitioning on branch and month, which are low cardinality and match how reports filter, giving a few thousand healthy directories with real pruning benefits, and we used bucketing by account id for the account-level lookups instead. So the way I state it in interviews is: partition on low-cardinality columns you actually filter on, keep the partition count in the thousands rather than the millions, and for high-cardinality keys use bucketing or a derived low-cardinality column rather than partitioning directly.
